solution: Rewrite the integrand with fractional powers as \(x^{1/2} + x^{-1/2}\) and apply the power rule \(\int x^n\,dx = \tfrac{x^{n+1}}{n+1}\) to each term. This gives \(\tfrac{x^{3/2}}{3/2} + \tfrac{x^{1/2}}{1/2} = \tfrac{2}{3}x^{3/2} + 2x^{1/2} + C\). Differentiating this back returns \(\tfrac{2}{3}\cdot\tfrac{3}{2}x^{1/2} + 2\cdot\tfrac{1}{2}x^{-1/2} = \sqrt{x} + \tfrac{1}{\sqrt{x}}\), which confirms the result.

Integrate the given derivative term by term: \(\int 4x^3\,dx = x^4\) and \(\int -3x^{-4}\,dx = \tfrac{-3x^{-3}}{-3} = \tfrac{1}{x^3}\), so \(f(x) = x^4 + \tfrac{1}{x^3} + C\). The condition \(f(2) = 0\) gives \(16 + \tfrac{1}{8} + C = 0\), hence \(C = -\tfrac{129}{8}\). Therefore \(f(x) = x^4 + \tfrac{1}{x^3} - \tfrac{129}{8}\); the alternative form \(x^3 + \tfrac{1}{x^4}\) can be rejected at once, since differentiating it gives \(3x^2 - \tfrac{4}{x^5}\) rather than \(4x^3 - \tfrac{3}{x^4}\).

Use the symmetry property \(\int_{-a}^{a} f(x)\,dx = 0\) for an odd function and \(\int_{-a}^{a} f(x)\,dx = 2\int_0^a f(x)\,dx\) for an even one. Here \(x^3\), \(x\cos x\) and \(\tan^5 x\) are all odd, so each contributes \(0\) over the symmetric interval \(\left[-\tfrac{\pi}{2}, \tfrac{\pi}{2}\right]\), leaving only the even term \(1\). Hence the value is \(\int_{-\pi/2}^{\pi/2} 1\,dx = \pi\). A quick check of the oddness: adding the integrand at \(x\) and at \(-x\) cancels the first three terms exactly and leaves \(2\), whose integral over \(\left[0, \tfrac{\pi}{2}\right]\) is again \(\pi\).

Apply the property \(\int_0^{a} f(x)\,dx = \int_0^{a} f(a-x)\,dx\) with \(a = \tfrac{\pi}{2}\). Since \(\sin\left(\tfrac{\pi}{2}-x\right) = \cos x\) and \(\cos\left(\tfrac{\pi}{2}-x\right) = \sin x\), the substitution turns the integrand into \(\log\left(\frac{4+3\cos x}{4+3\sin x}\right)\), which is the negative of the original because \(\log\tfrac{1}{t} = -\log t\). So \(I = -I\), giving \(2I = 0\) and hence \(I = 0\).

Observe that the numerator is exactly the derivative of the denominator: \(\frac{d}{dx}\left(x^{10} + 10^x\right) = 10x^9 + 10^x\log_e 10\). With the substitution \(t = x^{10} + 10^x\) the integral becomes \(\int\frac{dt}{t} = \log|t| + C\). Restoring \(t\) gives \(\log\left(x^{10} + 10^x\right) + C\). Any integral of the form \(\int\frac{f'(x)}{f(x)}dx\) produces a logarithm, so a bare polynomial or exponential answer cannot be right here.

Replace the \(1\) in the numerator by \(\sin^2 x + \cos^2 x\), so the integrand splits as \(\frac{\sin^2 x}{\sin^2 x\cos^2 x} + \frac{\cos^2 x}{\sin^2 x\cos^2 x} = \sec^2 x + \csc^2 x\). Integrating term by term gives \(\tan x - \cot x + C\), because \(\int\csc^2 x\,dx = -\cot x\). The minus sign is the whole point: differentiating \(\tan x + \cot x\) would give \(\sec^2 x - \csc^2 x\), which is not the integrand.

Split the fraction into two terms: \(\frac{\sin^2 x}{\sin^2 x\cos^2 x} - \frac{\cos^2 x}{\sin^2 x\cos^2 x} = \sec^2 x - \csc^2 x\). Integrating gives \(\tan x - (-\cot x) = \tan x + \cot x + C\), since \(\int\csc^2 x\,dx = -\cot x\). It is that internal minus sign which turns the subtraction in the integrand into a sum in the answer.

The factor \(e^x(1+x)\) is precisely \(\frac{d}{dx}\left(xe^x\right)\), which signals the substitution \(t = xe^x\). The integral then becomes \(\int\sec^2 t\,dt = \tan t + C\). Restoring \(t\) gives \(\tan\left(xe^x\right) + C\). The argument must remain the whole product \(xe^x\), since an answer in \(\tan(e^x)\) or \(\cot(e^x)\) alone does not differentiate back to the integrand.

Complete the square in the denominator: \(x^2 + 2x + 2 = (x+1)^2 + 1\). With \(t = x+1\), so that \(dt = dx\), the integral becomes \(\int\frac{dt}{t^2+1} = \tan^{-1}t + C\). Restoring \(t\) gives \(\tan^{-1}(x+1) + C\); no extra algebraic factor of \(x\) or \((x+1)\) appears, since the substitution is a pure shift.

Complete the square under the root: \(9x - 4x^2 = 4\left[\left(\tfrac{9}{8}\right)^2 - \left(x - \tfrac{9}{8}\right)^2\right]\), so \(\sqrt{9x-4x^2} = 2\sqrt{\left(\tfrac{9}{8}\right)^2 - \left(x-\tfrac{9}{8}\right)^2}\). The integral becomes \(\tfrac{1}{2}\int\frac{dt}{\sqrt{a^2-t^2}}\) with \(t = x - \tfrac{9}{8}\) and \(a = \tfrac{9}{8}\), which is \(\tfrac{1}{2}\sin^{-1}\left(\frac{x-9/8}{9/8}\right) + C = \tfrac{1}{2}\sin^{-1}\left(\frac{8x-9}{9}\right) + C\). Differentiating this returns \(\frac{1}{\sqrt{9x-4x^2}}\), whereas the near-identical form with \(\frac{9x-8}{9}\) inside the inverse sine does not.

Resolve into partial fractions by writing \(x = A(x-2) + B(x-1)\); putting \(x = 1\) gives \(A = -1\) and putting \(x = 2\) gives \(B = 2\), so \(\frac{x}{(x-1)(x-2)} = \frac{-1}{x-1} + \frac{2}{x-2}\). Integrating gives \(-\log|x-1| + 2\log|x-2| + C\), which combines into \(\log\left|\frac{(x-2)^2}{x-1}\right| + C\). The squared factor must be \(x-2\), since that is the term carrying the coefficient \(2\).

Split the integrand as \(\frac{1}{x(x^2+1)} = \frac{1}{x} - \frac{x}{x^2+1}\), which is verified by recombining the right side over the common denominator \(x(x^2+1)\). Integrating gives \(\log|x| - \tfrac{1}{2}\log(x^2+1) + C\), where the second term uses \(\int\frac{x\,dx}{x^2+1} = \tfrac{1}{2}\log(x^2+1)\). The minus sign between the two logarithms is essential, because the sum form differentiates to \(\frac{1}{x} + \frac{x}{x^2+1}\), a different function.

Substitute \(t = x^3\), so that \(dt = 3x^2\,dx\) and hence \(x^2\,dx = \tfrac{1}{3}\,dt\). The integral becomes \(\tfrac{1}{3}\int e^t\,dt = \tfrac{1}{3}e^t + C\). Restoring \(t\) gives \(\tfrac{1}{3}e^{x^3} + C\); the coefficient is \(\tfrac{1}{3}\) because the derivative of the exponent \(x^3\) supplies a factor of \(3\).

This matches the standard pattern \(\int e^x\left[f(x) + f'(x)\right]dx = e^x f(x) + C\). Expanding the bracket gives \(\sec x(1+\tan x) = \sec x + \sec x\tan x\), and since \(\frac{d}{dx}\sec x = \sec x\tan x\), the choice \(f(x) = \sec x\) fits exactly. Hence the integral is \(e^x\sec x + C\).

Use the standard result \(\int\sqrt{a^2+x^2}\,dx = \tfrac{x}{2}\sqrt{a^2+x^2} + \tfrac{a^2}{2}\log\left|x+\sqrt{a^2+x^2}\right| + C\), here with \(a = 1\). This gives \(\tfrac{x}{2}\sqrt{1+x^2} + \tfrac{1}{2}\log\left|x+\sqrt{1+x^2}\right| + C\). The tempting guess \(\tfrac{2}{3}(1+x^2)^{3/2}\) fails because \(\frac{d}{dx}(1+x^2)^{3/2} = 3x\sqrt{1+x^2}\) carries an extra factor of \(x\) that the integrand does not have.

Complete the square: \(x^2 - 8x + 7 = (x-4)^2 - 9\), so apply \(\int\sqrt{t^2-a^2}\,dt = \tfrac{t}{2}\sqrt{t^2-a^2} - \tfrac{a^2}{2}\log\left|t+\sqrt{t^2-a^2}\right| + C\) with \(t = x-4\) and \(a = 3\). This gives \(\tfrac{1}{2}(x-4)\sqrt{x^2-8x+7} - \tfrac{9}{2}\log\left|x-4+\sqrt{x^2-8x+7}\right| + C\). The logarithm's coefficient is \(-\tfrac{a^2}{2} = -\tfrac{9}{2}\), so neither \(+9\) nor \(-3\sqrt{2}\) will differentiate back to \(\sqrt{x^2-8x+7}\).
Since \(\int\frac{dx}{1+x^2} = \tan^{-1}x\), the value is \(\left[\tan^{-1}x\right]_{1}^{\sqrt{3}} = \tan^{-1}\sqrt{3} - \tan^{-1}1\). That is \(\tfrac{\pi}{3} - \tfrac{\pi}{4} = \tfrac{\pi}{12}\).

Write \(4 + 9x^2 = 9\left(x^2 + \tfrac{4}{9}\right)\), so the integral is \(\tfrac{1}{9}\int_{0}^{2/3}\frac{dx}{x^2 + \left(\tfrac{2}{3}\right)^2}\). Using \(\int\frac{dx}{x^2+a^2} = \tfrac{1}{a}\tan^{-1}\tfrac{x}{a}\) with \(a = \tfrac{2}{3}\) gives \(\tfrac{1}{9}\cdot\tfrac{3}{2}\left[\tan^{-1}\tfrac{3x}{2}\right]_{0}^{2/3} = \tfrac{1}{6}\left(\tan^{-1}1 - \tan^{-1}0\right)\). This evaluates to \(\tfrac{1}{6}\cdot\tfrac{\pi}{4} = \tfrac{\pi}{24}\).

By the Fundamental Theorem of Calculus, if \(f(x) = \int_{0}^{x} g(t)\,dt\) then \(f'(x) = g(x)\), the integrand evaluated at the upper limit. Here \(g(t) = t\sin t\), so \(f'(x) = x\sin x\). There is no need to evaluate the integral at all, but doing so confirms it: \(f(x) = \sin x - x\cos x\), whose derivative is \(\cos x - \cos x + x\sin x = x\sin x\).

Multiply numerator and denominator by \(e^x\) to clear the negative exponent, giving \(\int\frac{e^x\,dx}{e^{2x}+1}\). With \(t = e^x\), so \(dt = e^x\,dx\), this becomes \(\int\frac{dt}{1+t^2} = \tan^{-1}t + C\). Restoring \(t\) gives \(\tan^{-1}\left(e^x\right) + C\). A logarithmic answer would require the numerator to be the derivative of the denominator, which it is not here.

Write \(\cos 2x = \cos^2 x - \sin^2 x = (\cos x - \sin x)(\cos x + \sin x)\), so one factor cancels against the square in the denominator and leaves \(\int\frac{\cos x - \sin x}{\sin x + \cos x}\,dx\). The numerator is now exactly the derivative of the denominator, so with \(t = \sin x + \cos x\) the integral is \(\int\frac{dt}{t} = \log|t| + C\). Hence the value is \(\log|\sin x + \cos x| + C\); the companion form in \(\sin x - \cos x\) differentiates to a different expression.

Apply the property \(\int_{a}^{b} f(x)\,dx = \int_{a}^{b} f(a+b-x)\,dx\) to \(I = \int_{a}^{b} x\,f(x)\,dx\), which gives \(I = \int_{a}^{b} (a+b-x)\,f(a+b-x)\,dx\). The hypothesis \(f(a+b-x) = f(x)\) turns this into \(I = (a+b)\int_{a}^{b} f(x)\,dx - I\). Solving, \(2I = (a+b)\int_{a}^{b} f(x)\,dx\), so \(I = \frac{a+b}{2}\int_{a}^{b} f(x)\,dx\).
